position: end — also mid, before the main verb

senses.gloss: Quickly and efficiently; without unnecessary delay.
examples: The court wants the case resolved as *expeditiously* as possible.
Your refund will be processed *expeditiously*.
The city moved *expeditiously* to repair the water main.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*expensively dressed*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: In a way that costs a lot of money.
examples: She was *expensively* dressed in a gray wool coat.
The apartment was *expensively* remodeled last year.
They live *expensively* for two people on a teacher's salary.

senses.gloss: By means of experiments or as a trial.
examples: The theory has never been tested *experimentally*.
The drug is still being used *experimentally* in a few hospitals.
The school introduced the four-day week *experimentally* for one semester.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*expertly made*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: With great skill.
examples: The chef *expertly* filleted the fish in under a minute.
The furniture is *expertly* crafted from solid oak.
She handled the angry customers *expertly*.

senses.gloss: Clearly and directly, leaving no doubt.
examples: The contract *explicitly* says that pets are not allowed.
I told him *explicitly* not to touch the thermostat.
The law doesn't *explicitly* mention electric scooters.

senses.gloss: Suddenly and violently, like an explosion.
examples: The company grew *explosively* in its first two years.
The tank could react *explosively* if it overheats.
He laughed *explosively* and nearly spilled his coffee.

position: end — after the verb (*grow exponentially*); before its word in *exponentially more*

senses.gloss: Faster and faster, at an ever-increasing rate; by a very large amount.
examples: The number of users has grown *exponentially* since the launch.
Costs rise *exponentially* as you add more features.
The second exam was *exponentially* harder than the first.

senses.gloss: In a way that clearly shows feelings or meaning.
examples: She plays the cello very *expressively*.
He talks *expressively* with his hands.
Try to read the poem more *expressively* this time.

position: mid — before the verb or past participle
modifies: verbs, past participles and phrases of purpose (*expressly for*)

senses.gloss: Clearly and definitely, in words that leave no doubt.
examples: Smoking is *expressly* prohibited anywhere on campus.
The will *expressly* states that the house goes to her.

senses.gloss: For one particular purpose only.
examples: The app was designed *expressly* for people with poor eyesight.
She came to Chicago *expressly* to see the exhibit.

senses.gloss: In a very beautiful, delicate or refined way; also, intensely.
examples: The dress was *exquisitely* embroidered with silver thread.
The restaurant serves *exquisitely* prepared seafood.
The last few minutes of the game were *exquisitely* tense.

senses.gloss: Without preparation or notes.
examples: The senator lost her notes and spoke *extemporaneously* for twenty minutes.
Good debaters can argue *extemporaneously* on almost any topic.
The band played the final number *extemporaneously*.

position: end — also mid, before a past participle

senses.gloss: Over a large area or to a great extent; in detail.
examples: She has traveled *extensively* in South America.
The house was *extensively* damaged in the fire.
He has written *extensively* about the Civil War.

position: end — also mid, before a past participle

senses.gloss: On or from the outside of something, especially the body.
examples: This cream is to be applied *externally* only.
*Externally*, the car looks almost new.
The hard drive connects *externally* through a USB port.

senses.gloss: By people or organizations outside a company or institution.
examples: The job was advertised both internally and *externally*.
The accounts are audited *externally* every year.

position: before its word — *extra careful*; end in *pay extra*, *charge extra*
modifies: adjectives and adverbs; verbs of paying and charging
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *extra*
contrast: *An extra hour* and *extra cheese* are the adjective, not this adverb. Before an adjective the adverb means 'more than usual': *extra large* is a size, *extra careful* is very careful — not 'too' careful.

senses.gloss: More than usually; especially.
examples: Be *extra* careful on the stairs — they're icy.
I'll have a coffee, *extra* hot, please.
She worked *extra* hard before the finals.

senses.gloss: In addition to the usual amount or price.
examples: Delivery costs *extra*.
They charge *extra* for a room with a view.

position: end — also before its word (*extravagantly praised*)

senses.gloss: Spending more money than is sensible.
examples: They lived *extravagantly* until the money ran out.
He spent *extravagantly* on cars and parties.

senses.gloss: In a showy or excessive way; far beyond what is usual.
examples: The ballroom was *extravagantly* decorated with gold and crystal.
Critics *extravagantly* praised her first novel.

senses.gloss: In a very happy, lively and energetic way.
examples: The fans cheered *exuberantly* when the final whistle blew.
The kids ran *exuberantly* into the waves.
She waved *exuberantly* from the other side of the street.

senses.gloss: In a way that shows great joy at a success or victory.
examples: "We did it!" she shouted *exultantly*.
The team lifted the trophy *exultantly* over their heads.
He grinned *exultantly* as the results came in.

senses.gloss: Extremely, to an almost unbelievable degree.
examples: He's a *fabulously* wealthy real estate developer.
The show was *fabulously* successful on Broadway.
The hotel has a *fabulously* expensive rooftop bar.

contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective and always hyphenated: *a face-to-face meeting*. As an adverb you will see both *meet face-to-face* and *meet face to face*.

senses.gloss: In each other's physical presence, not by phone, email or video.
examples: We've talked on Zoom, but we've never met *face-to-face*.
Some things are better discussed *face-to-face*.

senses.gloss: come face-to-face with: to meet or confront someone or something directly.
examples: On the trail we came *face-to-face* with a black bear.
Working in the ER, she came *face-to-face* with the opioid crisis.

senses.gloss: Jokingly, often about something serious or at the wrong moment.
examples: "Maybe we should just move to Canada," he said *facetiously*.
I was speaking *facetiously* — I don't really want a third cat.
She *facetiously* suggested we hold the meeting at the beach.

ru: с точки зрения фактов, по фактам
type: viewpoint — with respect to the facts
contrast: A false friend: Russian *фактически* means 'in fact, actually' — that is *actually* or *in effect* in English. *Factually* only means 'in terms of facts': *The article is factually wrong*.

senses.gloss: In terms of the facts; as regards what is true.
senses.ru: с точки зрения фактов, по фактам
examples: The report is *factually* accurate but badly written.
His claim was *factually* incorrect.
The story is *factually* based, though the names have been changed.

position: before its word — *faintly amused*; end after a verb (*smiled faintly*)

senses.gloss: Slightly; a little.
examples: The kitchen smelled *faintly* of garlic.
He looked *faintly* embarrassed.
The idea seemed *faintly* ridiculous to me.

senses.gloss: Weakly; so that it is hard to see or hear.
examples: She smiled *faintly* but didn't say anything.
We could *faintly* hear music from next door.

position: end — also mid, before the verb
contrast: *Yours faithfully* is a British way to end a formal letter; Americans write *Sincerely* or *Sincerely yours*.

senses.gloss: Loyally and reliably, without stopping.
examples: He served the company *faithfully* for thirty years.
She *faithfully* calls her mother every Sunday.
My grandfather *faithfully* watched every Cubs game.

senses.gloss: Accurately; exactly as the original.
examples: The movie follows the book *faithfully*.
The old theater has been *faithfully* restored.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*falsely accused*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: Wrongly; in a way that is not true.
examples: He spent ten years in prison after being *falsely* accused.
The website *falsely* claimed the product was made in the USA.
Many people *falsely* believe that lightning never strikes twice.

senses.gloss: Hesitantly, stopping and starting, without confidence.
examples: He spoke *falteringly*, looking down at his notes.
She walked *falteringly* across the room on her new crutches.
The engine started *falteringly*, then died.

position: mid — before a past participle (*familiarly known as*); end after other verbs

senses.gloss: Informally, in everyday use — mostly in *familiarly known as*.
examples: Philadelphia is *familiarly* known as Philly.
The Federal National Mortgage Association, *familiarly* called Fannie Mae, buys home loans.

senses.gloss: In a very friendly, informal way, sometimes too much so.
examples: The new intern spoke to the CEO a little too *familiarly*.
He greeted everyone *familiarly* by their first names.

position: mid — before the verb (*famously said*); end in *get along famously*
comparison: more/most — *most famously* is common in the first sense

senses.gloss: As is well known; in a way that many people know about.
examples: Mark Twain *famously* said that the report of his death was an exaggeration.
The restaurant is *famously* difficult to get a table at.
He has written many books, most *famously* a series about a boy wizard.

senses.gloss: Very well — in *get along famously*.
examples: The two dogs got along *famously* from day one.
The two families got along *famously* at the wedding.

position: mid or end — before an adjective (*fanatically loyal*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: With extreme, unreasonable enthusiasm or devotion.
examples: The team has a *fanatically* loyal following.
He trains *fanatically*, even on vacation.
She is *fanatically* neat about her desk.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*fancifully named*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: In an imaginative or unusual way, not based on reality.
examples: The cocktails on the menu are *fancifully* named.
The walls were *fancifully* painted with dragons and castles.
Some historians have *fancifully* suggested that he never existed.

position: before its word — *fantastically rich*; end in the manner sense

senses.gloss: Extremely; to an unbelievable degree.
examples: The software is *fantastically* expensive.
She's a *fantastically* talented musician.
Their first album was *fantastically* successful.

senses.gloss: Extremely well.
examples: The kids did *fantastically* at the swim meet.
The new system works *fantastically*.

position: mid or end — before a past participle or adjective (*fashionably dressed*, *fashionably late*)
modifies: past participles, a few adjectives, and verbs

senses.gloss: In a way that follows current fashion.
examples: She's always *fashionably* dressed, even at the grocery store.
We arrived *fashionably* late, just after nine.
The loft is *fashionably* decorated with exposed brick and plants.

senses.gloss: With great, sometimes excessive care about detail, order or cleanliness.
examples: He *fastidiously* wiped down the counter after every use.
Her notes are *fastidiously* organized by date and topic.
The old car has been *fastidiously* maintained.

position: mid — before a past participle (*fatally wounded*, *fatally flawed*)

senses.gloss: In a way that causes death.
examples: Two people were *fatally* injured in the crash.
The officer was *fatally* shot while on duty.

senses.gloss: In a way that leads to failure or disaster.
examples: The plan was *fatally* flawed from the start.
The campaign was *fatally* weakened by the scandal.

senses.gloss: Without any mistakes.
examples: The pianist played the whole concerto *faultlessly*.
Everything went *faultlessly* on the day of the wedding.
She answered every question *faultlessly*.

position: end — also mid, before a past participle (*favorably impressed*)
contrast: *Favourably* is the British spelling. *Compare favorably with* means 'be as good as or better than', not 'be compared in a friendly way'.

senses.gloss: With approval; in a way that shows or gives an advantage.
examples: Critics reviewed the play *favorably*.
Our prices compare *favorably* with those of our competitors.
The committee was *favorably* impressed by her proposal.

senses.gloss: In a frightened or anxious way.
examples: The child looked *fearfully* at the big dog.
"Is someone there?" she asked *fearfully*.
Investors are watching the markets *fearfully*.

position: end — also mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: Without fear; bravely.
examples: The firefighters went *fearlessly* into the burning building.
She *fearlessly* spoke out against corruption.
Toddlers climb *fearlessly*, which is what scares their parents.

type: viewpoint — by or at the level of the national government

senses.gloss: By the federal government, or under federal law.
examples: The program is *federally* funded.
Minimum wage is set *federally*, but many states set a higher one.
Marijuana is legal in some states but still *federally* illegal.

senses.gloss: Weakly; without strength, energy or conviction.
examples: The kitten meowed *feebly* from under the porch.
He *feebly* protested, but nobody listened.
"It was a joke," she said *feebly*.

position: end — before its word as a degree adverb (*ferociously competitive*)

senses.gloss: In a fierce, violent way; also, extremely.
examples: The dog barked *ferociously* at the mail carrier.
Both teams fought *ferociously* for the ball.
The tech industry is *ferociously* competitive.

position: mid or end — before the verb (*fervently hope*) or after it

senses.gloss: With strong, sincere feeling.
examples: I *fervently* hope we never have to do that again.
She believes *fervently* in public education.
The crowd prayed *fervently* for rain.

position: end — also mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: Very quickly and with nervous excitement.
examples: Engineers worked *feverishly* to restore power.
He searched *feverishly* through his bag for his passport.
The staff were *feverishly* preparing for the inspection.

senses.gloss: Extremely — usually of something difficult or cleverly made.
examples: The Saturday crossword is *fiendishly* difficult.
It's a *fiendishly* clever plot.
The tax code is *fiendishly* complicated.

position: end — before its word as a degree adverb (*fiercely loyal*)

senses.gloss: In an angry, violent or aggressive way.
examples: The two candidates argued *fiercely* about taxes.
The wind blew *fiercely* all night.

senses.gloss: Very strongly; intensely.
examples: She is *fiercely* independent.
He's *fiercely* loyal to his friends.
The school is *fiercely* proud of its football team.

position: end — often in *figuratively speaking*; also front
contrast: *Figuratively* is the opposite of *literally*. In casual American speech *literally* is often used where *figuratively* is meant (*I literally died laughing*); careful writers avoid this.

senses.gloss: Not in the basic, literal meaning of the words; as a figure of speech.
examples: When I said he was a snake, I meant it *figuratively*.
The new mayor is, *figuratively* speaking, cleaning house.
The word *heart* is often used *figuratively* to mean courage.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *fine*
contrast: In *I'm fine* and *a fine day*, *fine* is the adjective. The adverb in *It works fine* is informal but completely normal in American speech; formal writing uses *well*. *Chop it fine* and *finely chopped* mean the same thing.

senses.gloss: Well; in a satisfactory way — informal.
examples: The old laptop still works *fine*.
Don't worry, you're doing *fine*.
Friday at two suits me *fine*.

senses.gloss: Into very small pieces or very thin lines.
examples: Chop the onion *fine* before adding it to the pan.
Grind the coffee *fine* for espresso.

position: mid or end — usually before a past participle (*finely chopped*)

senses.gloss: Into very small pieces or thin lines.
examples: Add two cloves of *finely* chopped garlic.
Top with *finely* grated Parmesan.

senses.gloss: Precisely and delicately; in careful detail.
examples: The engine is *finely* tuned for racing.
The two sides are *finely* balanced, so the vote could go either way.
It's a *finely* crafted novel.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *firm*
contrast: The flat adverb lives almost only in *stand firm* and *hold firm*. Everywhere else use *firmly*: *hold the rope firmly*, *I firmly believe*.

senses.gloss: Without changing your position or giving in.
examples: The union is standing *firm* on its demands.
Despite the pressure, the governor held *firm*.
Mortgage rates have held *firm* for three months.

position: mid or end — before the verb (*firmly believe*) or after the verb and object

senses.gloss: Tightly or securely, so that it does not move.
examples: Hold the handle *firmly* and pull.
Make sure the car seat is *firmly* attached.
Press the lid down *firmly* until it clicks.

senses.gloss: Strongly and definitely, without changing your mind.
examples: I *firmly* believe that everyone deserves a second chance.
"No more screens tonight," she said *firmly*.

ru: из первых рук, на собственном опыте

senses.gloss: Directly, from your own experience rather than from other people.
senses.ru: из первых рук, на собственном опыте
examples: I saw *firsthand* how hard nurses work.
Students learn about farming *firsthand* by working on the farm.
She knows *firsthand* what it's like to be homeless.

type: viewpoint — with respect to government or company money

senses.gloss: In terms of public money, taxes and budgets.
examples: She describes herself as *fiscally* conservative but socially liberal.
The mayor promised to be *fiscally* responsible with taxpayers' money.
The plan isn't *fiscally* sustainable in the long run.

senses.gloss: Irregularly, starting and stopping; not steadily.
examples: I slept *fitfully* on the overnight flight.
The fire burned *fitfully* in the wet wood.
The old generator ran *fitfully* all evening.

type: stance — a comment that something is appropriate; also manner
position: front — as a comment with a comma; mid before a past participle (*fittingly named*)

senses.gloss: In a way that is right or suitable for the situation.
examples: *Fittingly*, the award was presented in her hometown.
The dog is *fittingly* named Rocket.
The festival ended, *fittingly*, with a performance by local kids.

senses.gloss: Without moving the eyes; steadily.
examples: She stared *fixedly* at the phone, waiting for it to ring.
He looked *fixedly* out the window and didn't answer.
The cat watched the bird *fixedly* for ten minutes.

position: mid — before the verb, past participle or adjective (*flagrantly violated*, *flagrantly illegal*)

senses.gloss: In an obvious and shocking way — of breaking rules or laws.
examples: The company *flagrantly* violated safety regulations.
The referee ignored a *flagrantly* illegal hit.
He *flagrantly* disregarded the court's order.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*flamboyantly dressed*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: In a bold, colorful way that attracts attention.
examples: The singer was *flamboyantly* dressed in pink feathers.
He gestures *flamboyantly* when he tells a story.
The house is *flamboyantly* decorated for Halloween every year.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*flashily dressed*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: In a showy way meant to impress, often tastelessly.
examples: He was *flashily* dressed in a gold watch and a white suit.
The team plays *flashily*, but they don't win many games.
The casino is *flashily* lit with neon.

senses.gloss: Perfectly, without any mistakes or faults.
examples: The gymnast performed her routine *flawlessly*.
The software update installed *flawlessly*.
She speaks English *flawlessly*, with no accent at all.

senses.gloss: In a way that can change to suit different situations.
examples: Many employees now work *flexibly* from home.
The rules should be applied *flexibly*.
The funds can be used *flexibly* for any school project.

senses.gloss: Without the seriousness or respect a situation needs.
examples: "It's only money," he said *flippantly*.
She apologized for speaking so *flippantly* about the accident.
Don't answer the judge *flippantly*.

senses.gloss: In a way that playfully shows romantic interest.
examples: She smiled *flirtatiously* at him across the bar.
He winked *flirtatiously* and walked away.
They were chatting *flirtatiously* by the pool.

senses.gloss: Easily and without stopping — especially of speaking a language.
examples: She speaks Russian and Spanish *fluently*.
After a year abroad, he could read French *fluently*.
The more you practice, the more *fluently* you'll speak.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *flush*
contrast: The adjective *flush* means 'having plenty of money' (*flush with cash*); the verb means to wash out with water (*flush the toilet*) or to turn red in the face. Neither is this adverb.

senses.gloss: So as to be exactly level or in close contact with a surface.
examples: The new cabinets fit *flush* against the wall.
Mount the shelf *flush* with the edge of the counter.

senses.gloss: Directly and squarely — of a hit or blow.
examples: The punch caught him *flush* on the jaw.
He hit the ball *flush* and it sailed over the fence.

position: mid or end — before the verb (*fondly remember*) or after it
contrast: In older or literary English *fondly imagine* or *fondly believe* means 'foolishly and hopefully believe': *He fondly imagined she would wait for him*.

senses.gloss: With love and warm feelings.
examples: I remember my first teacher very *fondly*.
She smiled *fondly* at her grandchildren.
Locals still speak *fondly* of the old diner.

position: mid or end — also front as a comment (*Foolishly, I said yes*)

senses.gloss: In a silly or unwise way.
examples: I *foolishly* left my phone on the roof of the car.
*Foolishly*, we didn't check the weather before the hike.
He behaved *foolishly* at the party and regretted it.

modifies: verbs, especially of speaking and arguing
contrast: *Forcefully* is about strength and conviction: *She argued forcefully*. *Forcibly* is about physical force against someone's will: *He was forcibly removed*.

senses.gloss: Strongly and with conviction; with energy.
examples: She argued *forcefully* for a new approach.
The president spoke *forcefully* about the need for change.
He pushed the door *forcefully*, and it finally opened.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*forcibly removed*) or after the verb
contrast: *Forcibly* means 'using physical force'; *forcefully* means 'strongly, with conviction': *forcibly evicted* but *forcefully argued*.

senses.gloss: By using physical force, against someone's will.
examples: Two protesters were *forcibly* removed from the meeting.
Thousands of families were *forcibly* relocated.
The police had to open the door *forcibly*.

position: front — as *first and foremost*, usually with a comma
contrast: In *the world's foremost expert* (leading, most important) *foremost* is an adjective, not this adverb.

senses.gloss: first and foremost: most importantly; above all.
examples: *First and foremost*, I'm a mother.
The job is, *first and foremost*, about keeping people safe.
We need, *first and foremost*, a clear budget.

senses.gloss: In a sad, lonely and hopeless way.
examples: The puppy looked up at us *forlornly* from the shelter cage.
An old bicycle leaned *forlornly* against the fence.
He waited *forlornly* by the phone.

position: mid or end — before the verb (*formally announced*) or after it (*dress formally*)
contrast: A false friend: Russian *формально* often means 'only on paper, nominally' — that is *technically* or *nominally* in English. *Formally* means 'officially' or 'in a formal style': *He was formally charged* is a real, official charge.

senses.gloss: Officially, following the proper rules or procedure.
examples: The company *formally* announced the merger on Monday.
She was *formally* charged with fraud.
We haven't been *formally* introduced.

senses.gloss: In a formal style, not casually.
examples: Guests are asked to dress *formally*.
He always writes very *formally*, even in text messages.

senses.gloss: Impressively, to a degree that makes someone or something hard to deal with or beat.
examples: She's a *formidably* intelligent trial lawyer.
The team looks *formidably* strong this season.
The bar exam is *formidably* difficult.

modifies: verbs of movement and a few fixed phrases
contrast: *Forth* and *fourth* sound exactly the same. Outside fixed phrases (*back and forth*, *and so forth*, *set forth*) everyday English uses *forward* or *out*.

senses.gloss: back and forth: from one place or side to the other, again and again.
examples: He paced *back and forth* in the waiting room.
We emailed *back and forth* about the details all week.

senses.gloss: and so forth: and other similar things.
examples: Bring a towel, sunscreen, a hat, *and so forth*.
The fee covers books, lab equipment *and so forth*.

senses.gloss: Forward, out or away — formal, with verbs such as *set*, *go*, *come*, *bring*.
examples: The explorers set *forth* at dawn.
The report sets *forth* three possible solutions.
A spring of cold water gushed *forth* from the rock.

senses.gloss: from that day forth, from now forth: from that time on — formal.
examples: From that day *forth*, she never missed a practice.
From this moment *forth*, you are free.

senses.gloss: Directly and honestly, without hiding anything.
examples: The coach spoke *forthrightly* about the team's mistakes.
She answered the reporters' questions *forthrightly*.
The senator addressed the scandal more *forthrightly* than anyone expected.

senses.gloss: Immediately — formal and legal.
examples: The contract may be terminated *forthwith* if either party breaks these terms.
The judge ordered that the prisoner be released *forthwith*.
The resignation takes effect *forthwith*.

position: front — as a comment with a comma; also mid
contrast: Strictly, *fortuitously* means 'by chance', lucky or not. Most Americans now use it to mean 'luckily', and some careful writers object to that.

senses.gloss: By a lucky chance.
examples: *Fortuitously*, a doctor was sitting in the next row.
The meeting was *fortuitously* timed, just before the vote.
We *fortuitously* found a parking spot right in front.

senses.gloss: By four times as much.
examples: The price of eggs has increased *fourfold* in a year.
Online sales grew *fourfold* during the pandemic.
The risk rises almost *fourfold* for smokers.

position: end — also mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: In a hurried, desperate way, out of fear or worry.
examples: She searched *frantically* for her keys.
Parents were *frantically* calling the school.
The man waved *frantically* for help.

senses.gloss: By deceiving people, illegally, usually to get money.
examples: He *fraudulently* claimed unemployment benefits for two years.
The loans were obtained *fraudulently*.
Her signature was *fraudulently* used on the documents.

senses.gloss: To a strange or unnaturally extreme degree — informal.
examples: The new center is *freakishly* tall — almost seven foot four.
It was *freakishly* warm for February.
My little brother is *freakishly* good at math.

senses.gloss: In a fast, energetic and disorganized way.
examples: Waiters rushed *frenetically* between the tables.
The band played *frenetically* until midnight.
Reporters were typing *frenetically* as the results came in.

position: before its word — before *out of*, *from*, and a past participle
modifies: prepositional phrases (*fresh from*, *fresh out of*) and past participles
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *fresh*
contrast: In *fresh bread* and *fresh air*, *fresh* is the adjective. Before a participle the flat adverb is informal and usually hyphenated (*fresh-baked*, *fresh-squeezed*); *freshly baked* is the neutral form.

senses.gloss: Very recently; just.
examples: She's *fresh* out of law school.
The bread is *fresh* from the oven.
He came to the meeting *fresh* off a red-eye flight.

senses.gloss: fresh out of: having just sold or used up the last of something — informal.
examples: Sorry, we're *fresh* out of blueberry muffins.
I'm *fresh* out of ideas — any suggestions?

senses.gloss: Recently — before a past participle.
examples: The house smelled of *freshly* baked bread.
I'd like a glass of *freshly* squeezed orange juice.
Watch out — the bench is *freshly* painted.

senses.gloss: In a worried, restless or irritable way.
examples: The baby cried *fretfully* all night.
"What if we miss the flight?" she asked *fretfully*.
He paced *fretfully* outside the operating room.

senses.gloss: In a way that causes fear; alarmingly.
examples: The storm moved in *frighteningly* fast.
It's *frighteningly* easy to steal someone's identity online.
The water level rose *frighteningly* close to the top of the levee.

senses.gloss: In a silly, unserious way; wastefully.
examples: He spent his first paycheck *frivolously*.
The court fines people who file lawsuits *frivolously*.
She was criticized for talking *frivolously* about a serious issue.

senses.gloss: In a cold, unfriendly way.
examples: "That's none of your business," she replied *frostily*.
The proposal was received *frostily* by the board.
He nodded *frostily* and left the room.

senses.gloss: Carefully, spending as little money as possible.
examples: They lived *frugally* and paid off the house in ten years.
My grandparents ate *frugally* but never went hungry.
If we travel *frugally*, we can stay a whole month.

senses.gloss: In a way that produces good or useful results.
examples: The two labs have worked together *fruitfully* for years.
Your time could be spent more *fruitfully* on the second chapter.
The idea could *fruitfully* be applied to other cities.

senses.gloss: Without success; with no result.
examples: We searched *fruitlessly* for a gas station.
He spent months *fruitlessly* trying to get a refund.
The two sides negotiated *fruitlessly* until dawn.

ru: на полную ставку, полный рабочий день
type: duration — for a whole normal working week
contrast: Before a noun it is always hyphenated: *a full-time job*. As an adverb you will see both *work full-time* and *work full time*. The opposite is *part-time*.

senses.gloss: For the whole of a normal working or study week.
senses.ru: на полную ставку, полный рабочий день
examples: She works *full-time* and takes night classes.
He went back to work *full-time* after the baby turned one.
Most students here study *full-time*.

senses.gloss: In terms of how something works or what it does.
examples: The two phones are *functionally* identical.
The old building is *functionally* obsolete.

senses.gloss: For all practical purposes; in effect.
examples: Millions of adults are *functionally* illiterate.
Without a budget, the agency is *functionally* dead.

ru: в корне, коренным образом; по сути
position: before its word — *fundamentally different*; front with a comma in the second sense

senses.gloss: In a basic and very important way; completely.
examples: The internet *fundamentally* changed the way we shop.
Their approaches are *fundamentally* different.
I *fundamentally* disagree with that decision.

senses.gloss: At the most basic level; essentially.
examples: *Fundamentally*, he's a good person who made a bad choice.
The problem is *fundamentally* about money.

position: front — as *funnily enough*, with a comma
contrast: *Funnily enough* means 'strangely', not 'humorously'. In casual American speech *funny enough* is also common.

senses.gloss: funnily enough: strangely or surprisingly.
examples: *Funnily enough*, I was just thinking about you.
*Funnily enough*, the cheaper hotel was nicer.
We grew up on the same street, *funnily enough*.

senses.gloss: In a very angry way.
examples: "Get out of my office!" he shouted *furiously*.
She reacted *furiously* when she saw the bill.

senses.gloss: With great energy, speed or effort.
examples: He was typing *furiously* to meet the deadline.
The kids pedaled *furiously* up the hill.
The crew worked *furiously* to put out the fire.

senses.gloss: Secretly and nervously, trying not to be noticed.
examples: He glanced *furtively* at his phone during the meeting.
She *furtively* slipped the note into his pocket.
Two teenagers were smoking *furtively* behind the gym.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*fussily decorated*) or after the verb

senses.gloss: With too much attention to small, unimportant details.
examples: He *fussily* straightened every fork on the table.
She rearranged the pillows *fussily* before the guests arrived.

senses.gloss: With too much decoration or detail.
examples: The living room was *fussily* decorated with lace and china dolls.
The menu is *fussily* written, with three adjectives for every dish.

senses.gloss: Without any chance of success; in vain.
examples: He tried *futilely* to start the car in the freezing cold.
She searched *futilely* for her ring in the sand.
Neighbors *futilely* argued that the park should be saved.

position: mid or end — before a past participle (*gaily decorated*) or after the verb
contrast: Because *gay* now usually means 'homosexual', *gaily* sounds old-fashioned and is mostly met in writing. In speech Americans say *cheerfully* or *brightly*.

senses.gloss: Cheerfully and happily.
examples: The children sang *gaily* as they walked.
She waved *gaily* from the deck of the ship.

senses.gloss: In bright colors.
examples: The streets were *gaily* decorated for the festival.
Fishing boats were *gaily* painted in red and blue.

senses.gloss: gainfully employed: having a paid job.
examples: All three of her kids are now *gainfully* employed.
He hasn't been *gainfully* employed since the factory closed.
The program helps veterans become *gainfully* employed.
